title: The Man Who Lived With Baboons
book: Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst
author: Robert Sapolsky
wiifm: On a mental health ward you see behaviour that only makes sense if you know what happened one second, one hour, one year and one childhood before it. That is exactly how Behave works. It follows a single action backwards through the brain, hormones, upbringing, culture and evolution. You will travel with Robert Sapolsky from a lonely boyhood in Brooklyn to a Kenyan plain where he spent decades among baboons, and you will leave with a framework for understanding people at their best and worst that is useful at work, at home and on placement.

ch.h: A boy at the gorilla exhibit
b: Robert Morris Sapolsky was born on the sixth of April 1957 in Brooklyn, New York, the son of immigrants from the former Soviet Union. His father was an architect who restored old restaurants and buildings. The family was Orthodox Jewish, and the young Sapolsky took it seriously until, at around fourteen, he decided there was no God, no free will and no purpose built into the universe, a conclusion he has said he has held ever since.

He has described himself as an awkward, lonely child who spent hours at the American Museum of Natural History, especially in the hall of African mammals. By the age of twelve, so he has said, he was writing fan letters to primatologists. He wanted, quite precisely, to live in a museum diorama among the great apes.

Notice the two threads. One is a fascination with primates as mirrors of ourselves. The other is a conviction, formed in adolescence, that behaviour has causes all the way down. Behave, published forty-five years later, is where the two threads finally meet.

That loneliness, he has said, shaped his sympathy for the low-ranking and the bullied. The baboons he went on to study were not simply data. He gave them names from the Old Testament, Solomon, Saul, Benjamin, and wrote about their lives as if they were neighbours, which in a sense they were.
ch.cap: Young Robert presses against the museum gorilla diorama

b: Sapolsky studied biological anthropology at Harvard, graduating in 1978. Then, at twenty-one, he went to Kenya to study a troop of wild olive baboons in the Masai Mara, and he returned season after season for over two decades. His memoir of those years, A Primate's Memoir, is funny, tender and frequently alarming.

Between field seasons he earned a doctorate in neuroendocrinology at Rockefeller University in New York, under Bruce McEwen, studying how stress hormones affect the brain. That pairing was unusual and powerful. He would spend months darting baboons with anaesthetic to take blood samples and measure their stress hormones, then return to the laboratory to study what those same hormones did to neurons.

What he found among the baboons became famous. Low-ranking males, constantly harassed by those above them, had chronically raised levels of the stress hormone cortisol, higher blood pressure and worse cholesterol. Social rank was getting under their skin. Stress, he concluded, is not just an emotion. It is a physical event with physical costs, and in social animals much of it is caused by other members of the group.

Sapolsky turned these discoveries into a much-loved book, Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers, first published in 1994. A zebra running from a lion floods its body with stress hormones for a few minutes, and then it is over. Humans can trigger the same response for months by worrying about a mortgage, a manager or a social slight, and that, he argued, is why stress makes us ill. In 1987 he received a MacArthur Fellowship, the so-called genius grant.
ch.cap: Sapolsky darts a baboon on the Masai Mara

b: Then came the event he has called one of the most important things that ever happened in his scientific life. In the early 1980s a group of baboons in his study area, called Forest Troop, began raiding a rubbish dump at a tourist lodge. The most aggressive males pushed their way to the food, and the meat there turned out to be contaminated with tuberculosis. Within a short time those aggressive males were dead.

What remained was a troop with an unusual number of females and gentler males. And over the following years, something remarkable happened. The troop's culture changed. Aggression fell, grooming rose, and low-ranking animals were far less stressed. Most striking of all, young males who later joined the troop from outside, having grown up elsewhere, adopted the calmer style. Sapolsky and his colleague Lisa Share published the findings in 2004.

He draws a large lesson from a small troop. If even baboons, among the more aggressive primates, can develop a more peaceful culture that is passed on to newcomers, then human behaviour is not fixed by biology either. Biology sets the range. Circumstances and culture decide where in that range a group lands.

The story also carries a darker note. The tuberculosis outbreak did not only kill strangers. In A Primate's Memoir Sapolsky writes about losing baboons he had known and named for years, and he describes it as one of the great griefs of his life. It is part of why he writes about animals with such tenderness.
ch.cap: Gentle baboons groom where the bullies once fought

b: Behave was published in 2017, after decades of teaching a famous course in human behavioural biology at Stanford, where he became a professor. Its structure is its genius. Take a single behaviour, say a hand pulling a trigger or reaching out to comfort someone, and ask why it happened. Then keep stepping back in time.

One second before, the answer is in the brain. Sapolsky introduces the amygdala, central to fear and aggression, which can react to a threatening face in a fraction of a second, before we are aware of it. He introduces the insula, which handles gut disgust, both at rotten food and at moral violations. And he gives a starring role to the frontal cortex, the last part of the brain to mature, which helps us do the harder thing when it is the right thing.

The frontal cortex is not fully mature until around the mid-twenties. Sapolsky makes much of this. It means the region most responsible for restraint, planning and judgement is the one most shaped by experience, which is to say by everything that came before.

He also makes a memorable point about dopamine, which is often called the pleasure chemical. It is better understood as being about anticipation and pursuit. In experiments on monkeys, dopamine rises most not when a reward is certain but when it is uncertain, when the chance is around fifty per cent. Maybe, Sapolsky likes to say, is addictive. Anyone who has watched a gambler, or refreshed an inbox for a reply, will recognise it.
ch.cap: The amygdala flares before the frontal brake engages

b: Step back a little further. Seconds to minutes before an action, the senses have already been shaping it in ways we rarely notice. Sapolsky gathers studies on how faces, smells and surroundings tilt our choices, though he is careful to note that some of the subtle priming effects he describes have since struggled to replicate, a wider problem in psychology that he acknowledges.

Hours to days before, hormones are at work. Sapolsky spends time demolishing a myth about testosterone. It does not simply cause aggression. What it seems to do is amplify whatever behaviour wins status in a given setting. In a culture where status comes from generosity, more testosterone can, in some experiments, make people more generous. He also discusses oxytocin, often sold as the love hormone, and points out that it makes us kinder to our own group and can make us more suspicious of outsiders.

And he returns to stress. A little helps us focus. Prolonged stress damages the hippocampus, central to memory, and strengthens the amygdala, making people more fearful and more reactive. A stressed brain, in other words, is a brain primed for its worst behaviour.

He also discusses more ordinary influences, like hunger and fatigue. One well-known Israeli study from 2011 appeared to show that judges granted parole far more often after a meal break than just before one. Sapolsky uses it to show how bodily states can leak into serious decisions. Other researchers have since questioned that study, pointing out that the order of cases was not random, so its dramatic size is probably overstated even if the general point holds.
ch.cap: A hungry judge weighs parole just before lunch

b: Now step back further: to adolescence, childhood and even the womb. Sapolsky gathers evidence that childhood adversity, such as abuse, poverty and neglect, alters the developing brain in measurable ways, often enlarging the amygdala and weakening frontal control. Experiences in the womb, including maternal stress and malnutrition, can shape adult health and temperament.

He discusses genes too, and he is firm about what they do and do not do. Genes are not blueprints that fix behaviour. They are more like recipes whose results depend heavily on the kitchen. A famous example is a variant of a gene affecting the enzyme MAO A, which some studies linked to aggression, but only in men who had been maltreated as children. Sapolsky notes that even this finding has been contested and has not replicated reliably. The lesson he takes is the interaction itself: genes matter in particular environments.

For anyone in mental health nursing this is the most practical chapter. The person in front of you in crisis is reacting with a brain built over a lifetime, under conditions they did not choose. Understanding that is not excusing harm. It is the starting point for responding well.

Adolescence gets its own chapter, with the cheerful subtitle Dude, Where's My Frontal Cortex? Teenagers are not simply bad at judging risk. In laboratory studies they take far more risks when friends are watching than when alone, because the reward system is highly sensitive and the frontal brakes are still being built. It is also the age, Sapolsky notes, when people are most capable of idealism and sudden moral courage.
ch.cap: A teenager takes the risky jump as friends watch

b: Step back further still, to culture. Sapolsky compares societies and asks how history shapes behaviour. Collectivist cultures, many of them in East Asia with histories of rice farming that required cooperation, tend to emphasise harmony and the group. Individualist cultures emphasise the self. Herding cultures, where wealth could be stolen overnight, often developed cultures of honour, quick to defend reputation with violence, an idea he draws from research on the American South by Richard Nisbett and Dov Cohen.

Then evolution itself. Sapolsky reviews kin selection, reciprocal altruism and the evolution of cooperation, the same ideas we met with Dawkins, and he is generous to them while warning against using them as just-so stories that explain everything and predict nothing.
The point of this enormous zoom is to show that there is no single cause of any behaviour. There is a cascade, from milliseconds to millions of years, and each layer influences all the others.

Sapolsky is careful here not to romanticise or condemn any culture. Each pattern, he suggests, made sense in the conditions that produced it, and each carries costs as well as benefits. The useful question is not which culture is best but how the history of a group still shapes the reflexes of the people in it today.
ch.cap: Rice farmers cooperate while a herder guards cattle

b: In the second half of the book Sapolsky applies the framework to the big themes of human life, and the most important is our habit of dividing the world into us and them. He shows how quickly the brain does it: studies suggest the amygdala can respond differently to faces from another group within a tenth of a second. Children sort people into groups early. And in experiments, adults form loyalties to arbitrary groups based on almost nothing, such as a coin toss or a preference for one painter over another.

That sounds bleak, but Sapolsky stresses the hopeful side. The categories are remarkably flexible. Put people in a shared team, give them a common goal, and the dividing line moves. Studies of contact between groups, under the right conditions, show prejudice falling. The trick, he suggests, is not to abolish our tribal instincts, which may be impossible, but to keep widening who counts as us.

He also examines hierarchy, morality, empathy and violence, and the theme is always the same. Our best and our worst behaviour come from the same biology. Aggression that is horrifying in one context is admired as courage in another. The brain does not sort them for us.

Sapolsky is equally interesting on empathy. Feeling someone's pain, he points out, is not the same as helping them, and people swamped by another's distress often withdraw to protect themselves. What tends to produce effective help is a slightly cooler state: compassion that keeps some distance and asks what would actually make a difference. For carers and nurses facing suffering every day, it is a useful distinction.
ch.cap: A coin toss splits strangers into rival teams

b: The final part of the book is its most controversial. Sapolsky argues that once you see the full chain of causes, the idea of free will, in the sense of a choice that arises from nothing, becomes very hard to defend. He suggests our legal system should move away from retribution, punishing people because they deserve it, and towards something more like how we treat a car with faulty brakes: keeping others safe, without moral outrage.

He developed this further in his 2023 book, Determined. Many philosophers disagree. Compatibilists such as Daniel Dennett argue that free will, properly understood, is compatible with causation, and that responsibility remains a meaningful idea. Others worry that abandoning blame could undermine the motivation to behave well. This is a live debate, and Sapolsky is clear that he holds a minority position.

But even readers who reject his conclusion usually take away the softer version: that context matters enormously, that people are more shaped than they look, and that understanding why someone did something is not weakness but wisdom.
ch.cap: A car with faulty brakes is mended, not punished

b: Sapolsky, bearded and genial, remains one of the best-loved science teachers in the world. His Stanford lectures on human behavioural biology are watched by millions online. He has written about his own battle with depression, and about grief, with the same mixture of science and kindness.

His popular reputation also rests on a habit of honesty about uncertainty. In Behave he repeatedly stops to point out where a study is small, where a finding has not replicated, or where scientists simply do not know. That is unusual in a big popular book, and it is part of why the book has lasted while some of its individual findings have wobbled.

Behave leaves you with a simple discipline. When someone behaves at their worst, or at their best, ask what happened one second before, one hour before, one year before, and in their childhood. You will rarely find a single cause. You will almost always find more compassion, and better ideas about how to change what happens next.
ch.cap: Bearded Sapolsky lectures on the chain of causes

take: Trace a behaviour back through seconds, hours, years and upbringing. You will make better decisions about staff, clients and patients when you look past the moment.
Chronic stress makes people more fearful and reactive. Reduce needless pressure in your team and you will get calmer judgement and fewer conflicts.
Forest Troop became gentler and taught newcomers its ways. Deliberately set the norms of a team, and new hires will tend to adopt them.
Testosterone seems to boost whatever wins status locally. Reward cooperation and generosity, and competitive people will compete to show them.
Group lines are drawn fast but are flexible. Give people shared goals and shared wins to turn rivals into a team.
Most traits depend on environment as much as inheritance. Never write someone off on the basis of where they come from.
Knowing why someone acts badly lets you respond to keep everyone safe. It helps you act firmly without needless anger.
Some studies Sapolsky cites have not replicated. Use the framework confidently and hold specific experiments more loosely.
recall: What is the central structure of Behave?

Sapolsky takes a single behaviour and steps back through time, from brain activity one second before, through hormones, childhood, genes, culture and evolution. The point is that behaviour arises from a cascade of interacting causes.
What happened to Forest Troop, and why does it matter?

Its most aggressive males died after eating tuberculosis-infected meat at a lodge rubbish dump. The troop became calmer, and males who later joined adopted the gentler culture, showing that behaviour is not fixed by biology.
What does Sapolsky say testosterone really does?
It does not simply cause aggression. It seems to amplify whatever behaviour wins status in a given setting, so in some contexts it can increase generosity.
Why is the frontal cortex so important in his argument?
It handles restraint and judgement and is not fully mature until around the mid-twenties. Because it develops last, it is the brain region most shaped by experience and environment.
What is Sapolsky's controversial conclusion about free will, and who disagrees?

He argues that free will in the usual sense is not defensible, and that justice should focus on safety rather than retribution. Compatibilist philosophers such as Daniel Dennett disagree, holding that responsibility remains meaningful.
note: Sapolsky's childhood, Harvard degree and Kenyan fieldwork are described in his memoir A Primate's Memoir and in interviews. The Forest Troop findings were published by Sapolsky and Share in PLoS Biology in 2004. Some priming effects and the MAO A interaction he discusses have faced replication problems, which he acknowledges in part. His free will position, expanded in Determined in 2023, is a minority view among philosophers.

stories: The troop that lost its bullies

In the early 1980s a baboon group Robert Sapolsky was studying in Kenya, called Forest Troop, found a rubbish dump at a tourist lodge. The most aggressive males shoved their way to the food. The meat was contaminated with tuberculosis, and within a short time those males were dead. What was left was a troop of females and gentler males, and over the following years its culture changed: less aggression, more grooming, calmer low-ranking animals. The remarkable part came later. Young males who joined from other troops adopted the gentler style. Sapolsky and Lisa Share published it in 2004. If baboons can change their culture, so can we.

For more than twenty years Sapolsky darted wild baboons with anaesthetic to take blood samples and measure their stress hormones. The low-ranking males, constantly harassed by those above them, had higher cortisol, higher blood pressure and worse cholesterol. Rank was literally getting under their skin. He turned it into a book with a perfect title, Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers. A zebra fleeing a lion floods its body with stress hormones for a few minutes, and then it is over, one way or the other. Humans can switch on that same emergency response for months over a mortgage, a manager or a social slight. That, he argued, is why stress makes us ill.

In 2011 a study of Israeli parole boards seemed to show something alarming. Judges granted parole far more often just after a meal break than just before one, as if a prisoner's freedom depended on the timing of a sandwich. Sapolsky uses it in Behave to show how hunger and fatigue leak into serious decisions. Then comes the honest bit. Other researchers questioned the study, pointing out that the order of cases was not random, and that prisoners without lawyers tended to come last before a break. So the dramatic size of the effect is probably overstated. The general point, that bodily states affect judgement, still stands, and so does the lesson about checking shiny findings.
biz: Ask what came before the call

Many Debt Support Direct clients arrive after months of chronic stress, and Sapolsky shows what that does: a more fearful, reactive brain and weaker planning. A client who is short-tempered, evasive or misses calls is often not difficult but overwhelmed. This week, make sure every adviser and call handler can spot signs of vulnerability, record them, and adjust: slower pace, written summaries, a call back at a time the client chooses, and no decisions pushed on a first call. Then measure it: the share of clients with a recorded vulnerability, how many complete the advice process, and complaints. Consumer Duty expects exactly this.
Do not make applicants live on maybe

Sapolsky's finding that dopamine peaks when a reward is uncertain explains gambling and refreshing your inbox. Maybe is addictive, and it is also stressful. A homeowner waiting to hear about a loan is living on maybe. Never build suspense deliberately, and never imply approval is likely before a lender has decided. Instead, take the uncertainty away: tell each applicant exactly what happens next, when, and send a status update on WhatsApp at each stage, including a clear no when that is the answer. This week, measure the average time from enquiry to the first clear statement of next steps, and the number of days with no update.
connects: Sapolsky's split-second amygdala and slow frontal cortex map closely onto Kahneman's fast automatic System 1 and effortful System 2.

Marcus Aurelius reminds himself each morning that people who behave badly act from causes he can understand, much as Sapolsky argues that understanding a behaviour leads to less anger and better responses.
Behave's cascade of causes from milliseconds to millennia is a biological version of Meadows's warning that behaviour comes from the structure of a whole system, not a single trigger.
recap:
Start in Brooklyn in the nineteen sixties, with an awkward, lonely boy called Robert Sapolsky who spends hour after hour in the hall of African mammals at the natural history museum. By twelve, he says, he is writing fan letters to primatologists. At fourteen he decides there is no God and no free will, and that behaviour has causes all the way down.

At twenty one he flies to Kenya to study wild baboons, and he goes back season after season for more than twenty years. He darts them, takes their blood, and measures their stress hormones. The low-ranking males, bullied by those above them, are the most stressed and the least healthy. Rank gets under the skin. Stress, he concludes, is not just a feeling but a physical event with physical costs.

Then comes the story he calls one of the most important of his scientific life. The most aggressive males in one troop eat infected meat from a rubbish dump and die. The survivors build a calmer culture, and newcomers who join from outside adopt it. Biology sets the range. Culture decides where a group lands.

Behave, published in two thousand and seventeen, is built on one simple, brilliant idea. Take a single action and keep stepping back in time. One second before, the brain: the amygdala reacting to threat, the frontal cortex trying to do the harder, better thing. Hours before, hormones. Testosterone does not simply cause aggression; it amplifies whatever wins status in that setting. Years before, childhood, which shapes the very brain doing the choosing. Centuries before, culture. Millions of years before, evolution.

That is the first big idea: there is never one cause, only a cascade. The second is that chronic stress makes us more fearful and reactive. The third is that we split the world into us and them in a fraction of a second, but the line is flexible, and shared goals can move it. The fourth is that feeling someone's pain is not the same as helping them, and a cooler compassion helps more.

The fifth is the most controversial. Sapolsky argues that free will, in the sense of a choice from nowhere, does not survive the evidence, and that punishment should protect rather than avenge. Most philosophers disagree, and he admits his view is a minority one. He is just as honest when a study he likes fails to replicate.

So when someone behaves at their worst, or their best, ask what happened a second before, an hour before, a year before, and in their childhood. Here is the line to remember: understanding why someone acted is not excusing them, it is the beginning of responding well.
